**succepitque ignem foliis, atque arida circum**

*succepitque* (succipio, perfect, "and he caught/received"); *ignem* (ignis, acc. sg., "fire"); *foliis* (folium, abl. pl., "with leaves"); *arida* (aridus, neut. acc. pl., "dry things/tinder"); *circum* (adv., "around"). Achates catches the spark in leaves and places dry kindling around it to nurture the nascent flame.
176: **nutrimenta** (n. acc. pl., from *nutrimentum*) = "fuel, nourishment"; **dedit** (perf. 3rd sg., *do*) = "gave, provided"; **rapuit** (perf. 3rd sg., *rapio*) = "seized, snatched up"; **fomite** (m. abl. sg., *fomes*) = "tinder, kindling"; **flammam** (f. acc. sg., *flamma*) = "flame." He provided dry fuel (to the leaves mentioned in the previous line) and quickly caught/kindled a flame in the tinder.
177: **Tum** (adv.) "then"; **Cererem** (acc. sing., f.) "Ceres/grain," goddess of grain or metonymy for wheat; **corruptam** (perf. pass. part., acc. sing., f.) "spoiled, corrupted"; **undis** (abl. pl., f.) "by the waves/water"; **Cerealia** (adj., acc. pl., n.) "of Ceres, grain-related"; **arma** (acc. pl., n.) "tools, implements" (here, mills and ovens for processing grain). The Trojans prepare their wave-damaged grain and the implements of Ceres for making bread.
178: **expediunt** (verb, 3rd pl. pres. indic. of *expedio*) "they prepare, set out"; **fessi** (adj., nom. pl. masc., perf. pass. part. of *fatiscor/fateor*) "weary, exhausted"; **rerum** (noun, gen. pl. of *res*) "of affairs, circumstances"; **fruges** (noun, acc. pl. of *frux*) "grain, crops"; **receptas** (adj., acc. pl. fem., perf. pass. part. of *recipio*) "recovered, rescued." The weary sailors prepare the grain they have salvaged from the sea, readying it for drying and grinding despite its water-damaged state.

**et torrere parant flammis et frangere saxo.**

*torrere* (pres. act. inf., "to parch/roast") and *frangere* (pres. act. inf., "to break/crush") are complementary infinitives with *parant* (3rd pl. pres. act. indic., "they prepare"). *flammis* (abl. pl., "with flames") and *saxo* (abl. sg., "with stone/millstone") are ablatives of means. The Trojans prepare to roast and grind their recovered grain after their shipwreck.
180:
**Aeneas scopulum interea conscendit, et omnem**

*Aeneas* (nom. sg.): "Aeneas," subject. *scopulum* (acc. sg. m., *scopulus*): "cliff, crag," direct object. *interea* (adv.): "meanwhile." *conscendit* (3rd sg. pres./perf. indic., *conscendo*): "climbs, ascends." *omnem* (acc. sg. m./f., *omnis*): "all, the whole," modifying *prospectum* in the following line.

**Gloss on Target Line:**

*prospectum* (acc. sg. m., perfect passive participle of *prospicio*) "view, prospect"; *late* (adv.) "widely, far and wide"; *pelago* (abl. sg. n., *pelagus*) "over/on the sea"; *petit* (3rd sg. pres. indic. act., *peto*) "seeks, searches for"; *si quem* (conditional conj. + acc. sg. m., *quis/qui*) "if any(one)," introducing an indirect question depending on *videat*. Aeneas seeks a wide view over the sea to see if he might spot anyone—specifically Antheus or the other storm-tossed companions.
182:
**iactatum vento videat Phrygiasque biremis,**

*iactatum* (perf. pass. part. of iacio, acc. masc. sing.) "tossed, driven"; *vento* (abl. masc. sing.) "by the wind"; *videat* (pres. subj. 3rd sing. of video) "he might see"; *Phrygiasque* (adj. acc. fem. pl., -que = "and") "and Phrygian/Trojan"; *biremis* (acc. fem. pl.) "two-oared ships, biremes." Aeneas scans the sea hoping to spot Antheus or any other storm-tossed companion with their Trojan vessels.
183:
**aut Capyn, aut celsis in puppibus arma Caici.**

*aut...aut* (conjunction): "either...or"; *Capyn* (acc. sing., Greek name): Capys, one of Aeneas's companions; *celsis* (abl. pl., adj.): "lofty, high," modifying *puppibus*; *puppibus* (abl. pl.): "sterns, poops" of ships; *arma* (acc. pl., noun): "arms, weapons"; *Caici* (gen. sing., Greek name): "of Caicus," another Trojan companion. Aeneas surveys the sea hoping to spot either Capys or the weapons/insignia of Caicus on the high sterns of ships, but sees none of his scattered fleet.
184:
**Navem in conspectu nullam, tris litore cervos**

*Navem* (acc. sg. f., "ship") is the direct object negated by *nullam* (acc. sg. f., "no/not any"). *Conspectu* (abl. sg. m., "sight/view") follows the prepositional phrase *in conspectu* ("in sight"). *Tris* (acc. pl. m., "three," archaic/poetic form of *tres*) modifies *cervos* (acc. pl. m., "stags/deer"), while *litore* (abl. sg. m./n., "shore") indicates location. The verse contrasts the absence of ships with the presence of deer on the shore.
185: **prospicit** (verb, 3rd sg. pres. act. indic., *prospicere*) "he catches sight of" — **errantis** (verb, pres. act. part. acc. masc. pl., *errare*) "wandering" — **hos** (pronoun, acc. masc. pl.) "these" — **armenta** (noun, nom. neut. pl.) "herds" — **sequuntur** (verb, 3rd pl. pres. act. indic., *sequi*) "follow." Aeneas spies wandering stags; the entire herds follow behind these leaders.
186: **a tergo** (adverbial phrase: "from behind"); **longum agmen** (acc. neut. adj. + acc. neut. noun: "long column/train"); **vallis** (acc. fem. pl. or gen. fem. sg.: "valleys"); **pascitur** (3rd sg. pres. indic. pass. of *pascor*: "grazes/feeds"). The long train of animals grazes through the valleys from behind, extending the visual sequence of the wandering herd.
187: **Constitit** (perfect, 3rd singular of *consistere*) "he halted/took his stand"; **hic** (adverb) "here"; **arcumque** (*arcus*, accusative singular masculine) "and the bow"; **celerisque** (*celer*, accusative plural feminine) "and swift"; **sagittas** (*sagitta*, accusative plural feminine) "arrows." Aeneas stops and takes up the bow and swift arrows that his faithful companion Achates was carrying.
188:
**corripuit, fidus quae tela gerebat Achates;**

*corripuit* (3rd sg. perf. act. ind., *corripio*) "he snatched up"; *fidus* (nom. sg. m., adj.) "faithful"; *tela* (acc. pl. n., *telum*) "weapons/missiles"; *gerebat* (3rd sg. imperf. act. ind., *gero*) "was carrying"; *Achates* (nom. sg. m.) "Achates" (Aeneas's loyal companion). Aeneas seizes the bow and swift arrows that faithful Achates was bearing, preparing to hunt the deer whose leaders he will target first.
189:
**ductoresque ipsos primum, capita alta ferentis**

*ductoresque* (acc. pl. m., "and the leaders") – compound object with *ipsos* emphasizing the leaders themselves; *primum* (adv., "first") marks temporal priority in Aeneas's hunting; *capita alta* (acc. pl. n., "high heads," i.e., with lofty antlers) is the direct object of *ferentis* (acc. pl. m., pres. part. of *fero*, "bearing/carrying"), which modifies *ductoresque*. Aeneas first strikes down the stag-leaders themselves, distinguished by their towering antlers.
190:
**cornibus arboreis, sternit, tum volgus, et omnem**

*cornibus* (neuter ablative plural of *cornu*): "with horns," ablative of means. *arboreis* (ablative plural of *arboreus, -a, -um*): "tree-like, branching," modifying *cornibus*. *sternit* (3rd singular present active indicative of *sterno, -ere*): "he lays low, strikes down," describing the killing of stags. *volgus* (neuter accusative singular): "the common herd, the mass." Aeneas first kills the leaders with branching antlers, then massacres the entire herd of deer.
191:
**miscet** (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *misceō*) "throws into confusion"; **agens** (pres. act. participle of *agō*) "driving"; **telis** (abl. pl. of *tēlum*) "with weapons"; **nemora** (acc. pl. neut. of *nemus*) "groves/woodlands"; **turbam** (acc. sg. fem. of *turba*) "crowd/throng." 

Aeneas throws the crowd into confusion, driving them with weapons through the leafy groves; *agens* and *miscet* work together to depict active pursuit and disruption of the enemy forces amid wooded terrain.
192:
**nec prius absistit, quam septem ingentia victor**

*nec* (negative conjunction, "nor, and not"); *prius* (adverb, "before, sooner"); *absistit* (3rd sg. pres. indic. of *absisto*, "he ceases, withdraws"); *quam* (conjunction, "than, until"); *septem* (indeclinable numeral, "seven"); *ingentia* (neut. pl. acc. of *ingens*, "huge [bodies]"); *victor* (nom. sg., "victor, conqueror"). Aeneas does not cease his rampage until, as victor, he has slain seven huge warriors, matching the number of his ships (burned by the Latins).
193:
**corpora fundat humi, et numerum cum navibus aequet.**

*corpora* (n. acc. pl., "bodies") – direct object of *fundat*; *fundat* (3rd sg. pres. subj., "he lays low/pours out") – jussive subjunctive completing the action of *absistit*; *humi* (locative, "on the ground"); *numerum* (m. acc. sg., "the number") – direct object of *aequet*; *aequet* (3rd sg. pres. subj., "he may equal/match") – purpose or result clause. Aeneas slays seven stags, matching the number to his ships so each crew receives one.
194: **Hinc** (adverb) "from here/hence"; **portum** (accusative singular, m.) "harbor, port"; **petit** (3rd singular present active indicative, *peto*) "seeks, makes for"; **partitur** (3rd singular present deponent indicative, *partior*) "divides, distributes"; **socios** (accusative plural, m.) "companions, comrades" (object of distribution); **omnes** (accusative plural, m.) "all" (modifying an understood group). Aeneas departs from the site of the games and heads toward the harbor, distributing his companions/crews among all (the ships).
195: **Vina** (n. acc. pl., "wines") **bonus** (adj. nom. sg. m., "good/noble") **cadis** (n. abl. pl., "in jars") **onerarat** (v. plpf. 3rd sg., "had loaded") **Acestes** (n. nom. sg., "Acestes"). Aeneas distributes among all his comrades the wines which the good/noble hero Acestes had previously loaded into jars. The pluperfect indicates Acestes' prior hospitality on the Sicilian shore.
196:
**litore Trinacrio dederatque abeuntibus heros**

*litore* (n. abl. sg.) "on the shore," ablative of place where; *Trinacrio* (adj. abl. sg.) "Trinacrian/Sicilian," modifying *litore*; *dederat* (pluperfect 3rd sg. of *do*) "had given"; *-que* (enclitic conj.) "and"; *abeuntibus* (pres. part. dat./abl. pl. of *abeo*) "to those departing"; *heros* (nom. sg.) "the hero" (Acestes). Acestes, the hero, had given these wines on the Sicilian shore to the Trojans as they were departing.
197:
**dividit, et dictis maerentia pectora mulcet:**

*dividit* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *divido*) "he divides/distributes"; *dictis* (abl. pl. neut. of *dictum*) "with words"; *maerentia* (acc. pl. neut. pres. act. part. of *maereo*) "grieving/sorrowing"; *pectora* (acc. pl. neut. of *pectus*) "hearts/breasts"; *mulcet* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *mulceo*) "he soothes/calms." Aeneas distributes provisions on the Sicilian shore and soothes his men's grieving hearts with words of encouragement.
198:
**Target line: O socii—neque enim ignari sumus ante malorum—**

**socii** (nom. pl., *socius*, -ī, m.): "comrades, companions"; **ignari** (nom. pl. m., *ignarus*, -a, -um + gen.): "ignorant of, unacquainted with"; **sumus** (1st pl. pres. ind., *sum*): "we are"; **malorum** (gen. pl. n., *malum*, -ī): "of evils, misfortunes." 

Aeneas addresses his men as comrades who are not inexperienced in suffering, having endured previous hardships (*ante*).
199:
**O passi graviora, dabit deus his quoque finem.**

*passi* (perfect participle of *patior*, nominative plural masculine): "having suffered"; *graviora* (comparative neuter plural accusative of *gravis*): "more severe things, worse things"; *dabit* (future active indicative, third singular of *do*): "will give"; *finem* (accusative singular of *finis*): "an end." Aeneas addresses his companions as those who have endured even worse hardships, promising that god will grant an end even to these present troubles.
200:

251:
**navibus (infandum!) amissis, unius ob iram**

*navibus* (f. pl. abl.): "our ships," ablative absolute with *amissis*. *infandum* (n. acc. sg., gerundive of *for*): "unspeakable thing," exclamatory accusative. *amissis* (perf. pass. part., abl. pl.): "having been lost," completing the ablative absolute construction. *unius* (gen. sg.): "of one (goddess)," referring to Juno. *ob iram* (f. acc. sg.): "on account of (her) wrath," explaining the cause of their loss.
252:
**prodimur atque Italis longe disiungimur oris.**

*prodimur* (1st pl. pres. pass. indic. of *prodo*, "we are betrayed/abandoned"); *atque* (conj., "and"); *Italis* (abl. pl. adj. modifying *oris*, "from Italian"); *disiungimur* (1st pl. pres. pass. indic. of *disjungo*, "we are separated"); *oris* (abl. pl. of *ora*, "from shores/coasts"). Venus laments that the Trojans are betrayed and kept far from their destined Italian shores, expressing her complaint to Jupiter about their misfortunes.
253:
**Hic pietatis honos? Sic nos in sceptra reponis?**

*pietatis* (gen. sg., "of piety/devotion"); *honos* (nom. sg., "honor, reward"); *sic* (adv., "thus, in this way"); *sceptra* (acc. pl. neut., "scepters, kingdom, rule"); *reponis* (2nd sg. pres., "restore, replace"). 

Venus bitterly questions Jupiter: "Is this the reward for piety? Is this how you restore us to royal power?"
254: **Olli** (archaic dat. sg. of *ille*) "to her"; **subridens** (pres. part. nom. sg. m. of *subrideo*) "smiling"; **hominum** (gen. pl. of *homo*) "of men"; **sator** (nom. sg. m.) "sower, father, creator"; **deorum** (gen. pl. of *deus*) "of gods." Jupiter, the creator of men and gods, smiling at Venus, responds to her complaint with the serene countenance that calms heaven and storms.
255: **voltu** (abl. sg. m., *vultus*) "with expression/countenance"; **caelum** (acc. sg. n.) "sky/heaven"; **tempestatesque** (acc. pl. f., *tempestas* + *-que*) "and storms"; **serenat** (3rd sg. pres. ind. act., *sereno*) "he makes clear/calm." Jupiter reassures with the same look by which he clears the heavens and calms storms—a formulaic description of divine serenity and power over nature.
256: **oscula** (n. acc. pl., "kiss") **libavit** (perf. indic. 3rd sg. from *libo*, "he touched lightly, bestowed") **natae** (f. gen./dat. sg., "of/to his daughter") **dehinc** (adv., "then, thereafter") **fatur** (pres. indic. 3rd sg. deponent, "he speaks"). Jupiter bestows kisses upon his daughter Venus, then proceeds to speak the reassuring words that follow.
257:
**Parce metu, Cytherea: manent immota tuorum**

*Parce* (imperative of *parcere*, "spare" or "cease from") + *metu* (ablative of *metus*, "fear"); *Cytherea* (vocative, epithet for Venus, from her cult center Cythera); *manent* (3rd pl. pres. ind. of *manere*, "remain"); *immota* (nom. pl. neut. of *immotus*, "unmoved, unchanging"); *tuorum* (gen. pl. masc. of *tuus*, "your [people]"). Jupiter commands Venus to cease from fear, assuring her that the fates of her descendants remain fixed and unalterable.
258: **fata** (n. pl. acc.) "fates, destinies" – direct object of *cernes*; **tibi** (dat. sg.) "for you" – dative of reference; **cernes** (2nd sg. fut. act. indic. of *cernō*) "you will see"; **urbem** (f. sg. acc.) "city" – direct object, referring to Lavinium; **promissa** (n. pl. acc., perf. pass. partic. of *prōmittō*) "promised things, promises" – substantive participle, second object of *cernes*; **Lavini** (gen. sg.) "of Lavinium" – genitive modifying both *urbem* and *promissa*. Jupiter assures Venus that she will witness the fulfillment of destiny: both the city of Lavinium and the promises made concerning it.
259: **moenia** (n. acc. pl., "walls/fortifications") – object of *feres*; **sublimem** (adj. acc. sg. m., "exalted/raised on high") – modifying *Aenean* from the next line; **feres** (2nd sg. fut. act., "you will carry/bear") – main verb; **sidera** (n. acc. pl., "stars") – *ad sidera caeli* forms a prepositional phrase indicating destination; **caeli** (gen. sg., "of heaven/the sky") – modifying *sidera*. Jupiter promises Venus that she will see Lavinium's walls and will bear great-souled Aeneas aloft to the stars of heaven, confirming his apotheosis.
260: **magnanimum** (adj., acc. sg. masc.) "great-souled, noble-hearted" — **Aenean** (proper noun, acc. sg.) "Aeneas" (Greek accusative form) — **neque** (conj.) "nor, and not" — **sententia** (noun, nom. sg. fem.) "opinion, resolve, intention" — **vertit** (verb, 3rd sg. pres. ind. act.) "turns, changes." Jupiter assures Venus he will exalt "great-souled Aeneas" to the stars, declaring emphatically that his divine plan (*sententia*) remains unchanged.
261: **Hic tibi** (adverb + dative pronoun) "here to you" or "in this place for you"; **fabor** (1st sg. future indicative, *for*) "I shall speak"; **enim** (postpositive conjunction) "for, indeed"; **quando** (causal conjunction) "since"; **cura** (nominative sg.) "care, anxiety"; **remordet** (3rd sg. present indicative, *remordeo*) "gnaws at, troubles." Jupiter begins his prophecy to Venus, promising to speak since her anxiety troubles her.
262: **longius** (adv., comparative of *longe*) "further, at greater length"; **volvens** (pres. part., nom. sg. masc. of *volvo*) "unrolling, revealing"; **fatorum** (gen. pl. of *fatum*) "of the fates, of destiny"; **arcana** (acc. pl. neut. of *arcanus*) "secrets, mysteries"; **movebo** (fut. 1st sg. of *moveo*) "I shall set in motion, relate." The Sibyl promises to unfold at greater length the hidden secrets of fate, using the metaphor of unrolling a scroll (*volvens*) to describe revealing prophetic knowledge.
263: **bellum** (n., acc. sing.) "war"; **ingens** (adj., acc. sing.) "huge, mighty"; **geret** (v., fut. 3rd sing., from *gero*) "he will wage"; **Italia** (n., abl. sing.) "in Italy"; **populos** (acc. pl.) "peoples"; **feroces** (adj., acc. pl.) "fierce, savage." Jupiter prophesies that Aeneas will wage a great war in Italy against fierce peoples, setting the stage for the conflict with the Latins and Rutulians.
264: **contundet** (verb, future tense, 3rd singular) "will crush/shatter"; **mores** (noun, accusative plural) "customs/laws"; **viris** (noun, dative plural) "for the men"; **moenia** (noun, accusative plural) "walls/fortifications"; **ponet** (verb, future tense, 3rd singular) "will establish/set down." The subject (presumably Aeneas) will crush his enemies and establish both civic institutions (customs) and physical defenses (walls) for his people in Latium.
265:
**tertia dum Latio regnantem viderit aestas**

*tertia* (adj., nom. fem. sing.) "third"; *dum* (conj.) "until, while"; *Latio* (n., abl. sing.) "in Latium"; *regnantem* (pres. part., acc. masc. sing.) "ruling, reigning"; *viderit* (perf. subj., 3rd sing.) "shall have seen"; *aestas* (n., nom. fem. sing.) "summer, year." 

The line means "until the third summer shall have seen [him] reigning in Latium," marking the temporal duration of Aeneas's required military campaigns before establishing permanent peace.
266:
**ternaque transierint Rutulis hiberna subactis.**

*terna* (distributive numeral, nom. n. pl.) "three each" or "three"; *transierint* (perf. subj. 3rd pl., *transeo*) "shall have passed"; *Rutulis* (dat./abl. m. pl.) "for/by the Rutulians"; *hiberna* (nom. n. pl.) "winters"; *subactis* (perf. pass. part., abl. m. pl., *subigo*) "having been subdued/conquered." Three winters shall have passed with the Rutulians subdued, completing a temporal condition of three years (summers and winters) of Aeneas' reign in Latium.
267:
**At puer Ascanius, cui nunc cognomen Iulo**

*At* (conj., "but"); *puer* (nom. sg., "boy"); *Ascanius* (nom. sg., proper name in apposition); *cui* (dat. sg. rel. pron., "to whom"); *cognomen* (nom. sg., "surname, additional name"); *Iulo* (dat. sg., "Iulus"). Virgil transitions to Ascanius, explaining that he now bears the cognomen Iulus (the ancestor claimed by the Julian gens).
268:
**additur** (verb, 3rd sg. pres. pass. indic.) "is added" — **Ilus** (proper noun, nom. sg.) "Ilus" (original name of Ascanius) — **dum** (conjunction) "while" — **res** (noun, nom. sg. f.) "the power/state" — **stetit** (verb, 3rd sg. perf. act. indic.) "stood, endured" — **Ilia** (adjective, abl. sg. f.) "Ilian, Trojan" — **regno** (noun, abl. sg. n.) "in/under the kingdom."

The line explains that Ascanius was called Ilus while Troy's power still stood; the name Iulo/Iulus was added later, creating an etymological connection to the Julian family.
269:
**triginta magnos volvendis mensibus orbis**

*triginta* (indeclinable numeral) "thirty"; *magnos* (adj., acc. masc. pl.) "great," modifying *orbis*; *volvendis* (gerundive of *volvo*, abl. masc./neut. pl.) "by rolling" or "as they roll," expressing time within which; *mensibus* (noun, abl. masc. pl.) "by months," ablative of time; *orbis* (noun, acc. masc. pl.) "circles" or "cycles" (of years). The phrase means "thirty great cycles as the months roll by," i.e., thirty years.
270:
**imperio explebit, regnumque ab sede Lavini**

*imperio* (n., abl. sg.) "with rule/sovereignty" – ablative of means with *explebit*. *explebit* (v., fut. 3rd sg.) "he will complete/fulfill" – from *expleo*. *regnumque* (n., acc. sg.) "and the kingdom" – *-que* enclitic coordinating this clause with the previous. *sede* (n., abl. sg.) "from the seat/throne" – ablative of separation with *ab*. *Lavini* (adj., gen. sg. n.) "of Lavinium" – modifying *sede*. The subject (Ascanius) will complete his reign and transfer the kingdom from Lavinium to Alba Longa.
271:
**Gloss on Aeneid 1.271:**

*transferet* (3rd sg. fut. act., "will transfer") — the subject (Ascanius) will move the kingdom; *longam* (acc. sg. fem., "long" or "extensive") modifies *Albam*; *multa vi* (abl. sg., "with great force/power") — instrumental ablative indicating means; *muniet* (3rd sg. fut. act., "will fortify") — describing the strengthening of the new city; *Albam* (acc. sg., "Alba [Longa]") — direct object, the famous city Ascanius will establish and fortify after transferring rule from Lavinium.
272: **Hic** (adverb) "here" (at Lavinium); **ter centum** (numeral) "three hundred," modifying *annos*; **totos** (adjective, accusative masculine plural) "whole, entire," agreeing with *annos*; **regnabitur** (verb, future passive) "it will be ruled/reigned over"; **annos** (noun, accusative plural) "years," accusative of duration of time. The line describes the span of Alban kingship at Lavinium lasting three hundred full years before the dynasty relocates.
273: **gente** (abl. sing. f., *gens*) "under the race/people," **Hectorea** (abl. sing. f. adj.) "Hectorean, of Hector," **donec** (conj.) "until," **regina** (nom. sing. f.) "queen/royal," **sacerdos** (nom. sing. f.) "priestess." The realm will be ruled under Hector's Trojan lineage for three hundred years, until the royal priestess (Rhea Silvia) bears twin offspring.
274:
**Marte gravis, geminam partu dabit Ilia prolem.**

*Marte* (ablative of *Mars*): "by Mars" or "pregnant by Mars," indicating divine paternity. *gravis* (nominative feminine singular adjective): "heavy" or "pregnant with." *geminam* (accusative feminine singular adjective): "twin." *partu* (ablative of *partus*): "in/by birth." *Ilia* (nominative proper name): Rhea Silvia, the Vestal priestess. *prolem* (accusative of *proles*): "offspring." The priestess Ilia, pregnant by Mars, will give birth to twin offspring (Romulus and Remus).
275:
**Target:** *Inde lupae fulvo nutricis tegmine laetus*

**Gloss:** *inde* (adverb) = "then, thereafter"; *lupae* (noun, genitive singular) = "of the she-wolf"; *fulvo* (adjective, ablative singular neuter) = "tawny, tawny-yellow"; *nutricis* (noun, genitive singular) = "of the nurse"; *tegmine* (noun, ablative singular) = "with/in the covering, hide"; *laetus* (adjective, nominative singular masculine) = "joyful, proud." Romulus will be proud in the tawny hide of his nurse, the she-wolf, referring to the legendary she-wolf who suckled Romulus and Remus.
276: **Romulus** (nom. sg. m.) "Romulus" – subject; **excipiet** (3rd sg. fut. act., excipio) "will receive/take up" – main verb; **gentem** (acc. sg. f.) "the race/people" – direct object; **Mavortia** (acc. pl. n., adj. from Mavors = Mars) "Martian, of Mars" – modifying *moenia*; **condet** (3rd sg. fut. act., condo) "will found/establish" – second main verb. Romulus will receive the Trojan-descended people and found walls sacred to Mars, his divine father.
277: **moenia** (n. acc. pl., "walls, fortifications") – direct object of *condet* (understood from previous line); **Romanosque** (m. acc. pl., "and the Romans") – accusative direct object of *dicet*, coordinate with *moenia*; **suo de nomine** (abl. sg., "from his own name") – ablative of source with preposition *de*, modifying *dicet*; **dicet** (3rd sg. fut. act., "he will name/call") – main verb. Romulus will found the walls and name the Romans after his own name.
278:
**His ego nec metas rerum nec tempora pono;**

*His* (dat. pl. of *hic*) "for these/them" (i.e., the Romans); *metas* (acc. pl. f.) "boundaries, limits"; *rerum* (gen. pl. of *res*) "of things, of power"; *tempora* (acc. pl. n.) "times, temporal limits"; *pono* (1st sg. pres. act. indic. of *pono*) "I place, set." Jupiter declares he places neither spatial nor temporal limits on Roman dominion.
279: **imperium** (n., acc. sing.) "empire, rule"; **sine** (prep. + abl.) "without"; **fine** (n., abl. sing.) "end, limit"; **dedi** (vb., 1st sg. perf. act.) "I have given"; **Quin** (adv.) "Indeed, moreover"; **aspera** (adj., nom. sing. fem.) "harsh, fierce"; **Iuno** (n., nom. sing.) "Juno." Jupiter declares he has granted Rome limitless dominion, then pivots to acknowledge even hostile Juno's future change of heart.
280:
**quae mare nunc terrasque metu caelumque fatigat**

*quae* (relative pronoun, nom. fem. sing.) = "who," referring to Juno; *mare* (noun, acc. neut. sing.) = "sea"; *terrasque* (noun, acc. fem. pl. + enclitic -que) = "and lands"; *metu* (noun, abl. masc. sing.) = "with fear/dread"; *caelumque* (noun, acc. neut. sing. + -que) = "and heaven"; *fatigat* (verb, 3rd sing. pres. act. indic.) = "wearies, harasses." Jupiter describes Juno's current hostility: she now troubles sea, land, and sky with her fearful menace.
281:
**Target line: consilia in melius referet, mecumque fovebit**

**Key words:**
- *consilia* (n. acc. pl. of *consilium*): "plans, purposes"
- *melius* (n. acc. sg. of *melior*, comparative adj. used substantively): "better things, what is better"
- *referet* (3rd sg. fut. act. indic. of *refero*): "will turn, will direct"
- *fovebit* (3rd sg. fut. act. indic. of *foveo*): "will cherish, will favor"

Jupiter promises that Juno will turn her hostile designs toward better ends and will join him in cherishing the Romans, the future masters of the world and the toga-wearing race.
282:
**Romanos rerum dominos gentemque togatam:**

*Romanos* (acc. pl. m., "Romans") and *gentem* (acc. sg. f., "race/nation") with *togatam* (acc. sg. f., "toga-clad") are objects of an implied verb; *rerum* (gen. pl., "of things/affairs") modifies *dominos* (acc. pl. m., "masters/lords"). Jupiter prophesies the Romans as masters of the world and the toga-wearing nation, emphasizing their imperial destiny and civic identity through the distinctive Roman garment.
283:
**sic placitum. Veniet lustris labentibus aetas,**

*sic* (adverb): "thus, in this way"; *placitum* (neuter perfect passive participle of *placeo*): "it has been decided/decreed"; *veniet* (3rd sg. future active of *venio*): "will come"; *lustris labentibus* (ablative absolute, *lustrum* = five-year period, *labor* = glide/slip by): "as the five-year periods glide by"; *aetas* (nominative singular): "age, era, time." Jupiter prophesies that a destined time will arrive as the years pass.
284:
**Target line**: *cum domus Assaraci Phthiam clarasque Mycenas*

**Key words**: *domus* (nom. sg., "house/dynasty"); *Assaraci* (gen. sg., "of Assaracus," Trojan ancestor); *Phthiam* (acc. sg., "Phthia," Achilles' homeland); *claras* (acc. pl. fem., "famous"); *Mycenas* (acc. pl., "Mycenae," Agamemnon's city). 

Jupiter prophesies that the time will come when the Trojan house of Assaracus will subjugate Phthia and glorious Mycenae, reversing the outcome of the Trojan War.
285: **servitio** (n., abl. sing.) "by servitude/slavery"; **premet** (vb., fut. 3rd sing. from *premo*) "will oppress/press down"; **victis** (adj./ppl., abl. pl. from *vinco*) "conquered/defeated"; **dominabitur** (vb., fut. 3rd sing. deponent) "will rule over"; **Argis** (n., abl. pl.) "Argos" (here representing Greece). The Trojan Caesar will subject the house of Assaracus' Greek conquerors (Phthia and Mycenae) to slavery and rule over the once-victorious Argives.
286:
**Nascetur pulchra Troianus origine Caesar**

*Nascetur* (3rd sing. fut. pass. of *nascor*) "will be born"; *pulchra* (abl. sing. fem. of *pulcher*) "from beautiful/glorious"; *Troianus* (nom. sing. masc. adj.) "Trojan"; *origine* (abl. sing. of *origo*) "from origin/descent"; *Caesar* (nom. sing.) "Caesar" (referring to Julius Caesar or Augustus). A Trojan Caesar will be born from glorious lineage, continuing Virgil's prophecy of Rome's destined rulers descended from Troy.
287: **imperium** (n., acc. sing.) "empire, power" — **Oceano** (m., abl. sing.) "by/with the ocean" — **famam** (f., acc. sing.) "fame, renown" — **terminet** (3rd sing. pres. subj. of *termino*) "he may bound, limit" — **astris** (n., abl. pl.) "by/with the stars." The line describes one who will bound his empire by the ocean and his fame by the stars, with both accusative objects governed by *terminet* and the ablatives expressing extent or limit.
288: **Iulius** (nominative singular, proper name) "Julius," **a** (preposition + ablative) "from," **magno** (ablative singular adjective) "great," **demissum** (perfect passive participle, accusative singular neuter) "descended/derived," **nomen** (accusative singular noun) "name," **Iulo** (ablative singular, proper name) "Iulus." The line identifies Julius (Caesar) as bearing a name descended from great Iulus (Ascanius), establishing the Julian gens' divine Trojan ancestry through Aeneas's son.
289: **Hunc** (acc. sg. masc. of *hic*) "this man" (referring to Augustus); **caelo** (dat./abl. sg. of *caelum*) "to/in heaven"; **spoliis** (abl. pl. of *spolium*) "with spoils"; **Orientis** (gen. sg. of *Oriens*) "of the East"; **onustum** (acc. sg. masc. perfect passive participle of *onero*) "laden, burdened." Anchises prophesies that this figure (Augustus) will one day be received into heaven, laden with the spoils of the Orient after his conquests.
290: **accipies** (2nd sg. fut. act., *accipio*) "you will receive"; **secura** (nom./abl. sg. fem., *securus*) "free from care, at peace"; **vocabitur** (3rd sg. fut. pass., *voco*) "will be called upon/invoked"; **votis** (abl. pl., *votum*) "in prayers/vows." Jupiter prophesies that Venus will receive this future Augustus peacefully into heaven, where he too will be invoked in worshippers' prayers, like the established gods.
291: **Aspera** (adj. nom. pl. n.) "harsh, rough"; **positis** (perf. pass. part. abl. pl. n. from *pono*) "having been laid aside"; **mitescent** (fut. act. ind. 3rd pl. from *mitesco*) "will grow mild, will soften"; **saecula** (nom. pl. n.) "ages, generations"; **bellis** (abl. pl. n.) "wars." The harsh ages will grow gentle once wars have been set aside—a prophecy of Augustan peace following civil conflict.
292: **cana** (adj. nom. sg. fem.) "white/hoary" modifies **Fides** (nom. sg. fem.) "Faith/Good Faith" (personified goddess). **Vesta** (nom. sg. fem.) "Vesta" (goddess of the hearth), and **Quirinus** (nom. sg. masc.) "Quirinus" (deified Romulus) **cum fratre Remo** (abl. sg. masc.) "with his brother Remus" form a series of subjects who will give laws in the new Golden Age. The personified virtues and deified founders of Rome symbolize the restoration of ancient religious and moral order.
293: **iura** (n. nom./acc. pl. of *ius*) "laws, rights"; **dabunt** (3rd pl. fut. act. indic. of *do*) "will give, will establish"; **dirae** (adj. f. nom. pl. modifying *portae*) "dreadful, dire"; **ferro** (n. abl. sg. of *ferrum*) "with iron"; **compagibus** (f. abl. pl. of *compages*) "with fastenings, joints"; **artis** (adj. f. abl. pl. of *artus*) "tight, close-fitting." Faith and Vesta with Quirinus will establish laws; the dreadful gates [of War] will be closed tight with iron and fastenings.
294:
**Line:** *claudentur Belli portae; Furor impius intus,*

**Key Words:**
- *claudentur* (verb, future passive indicative, 3rd pl.): "will be closed"
- *Belli* (noun, genitive sg.): "of War" (personified)
- *portae* (noun, nominative pl.): "gates"
- *Furor* (noun, nominative sg.): "Rage/Frenzy" (personified)
- *impius* (adj., nominative sg. masc.): "impious, wicked"

The gates of the temple of War will be closed (symbolizing peace), while wicked Rage remains imprisoned inside. This prophesies the Pax Augusta, when Rome's civil wars would end.
295:
**saeva sedens super arma, et centum vinctus aenis**

*saeva* (adj., nom. sg. m., modifying Furor): "savage, fierce"; *sedens* (pres. part., nom. sg. m.): "sitting"; *super* (prep. + acc.): "upon"; *arma* (n., acc. pl.): "arms, weapons"; *vinctus* (perf. pass. part., nom. sg. m.): "bound, fettered"; *aenis* (adj., abl. pl. f., modifying a noun like *catenis* understood): "of bronze." Furor sits savagely upon weapons, bound by a hundred bronze chains.
296:
**post tergum nodis, fremet horridus ore cruento.**

*post* (prep. + acc.): "behind"; *tergum* (acc. n.): "back"; *nodis* (abl. m. pl.): "with knots/chains"; *fremet* (fut. 3rd sg.): "will roar/rage"; *horridus* (nom. m. sg.): "bristling, dreadful"; *ore cruento* (abl. n. sg.): "with bloody mouth." 

War personified sits bound with bronze chains fastened behind his back, yet will roar terrifyingly with bloodstained mouth—depicting restrained violence still menacing.
297:
**Haec ait, et Maia genitum demittit ab alto,**

*Haec* (nom. neut. pl., "these things") serves as object of *ait* (3rd sg. pres., "says/speaks"). *Maia genitum* (acc. sg. masc., "born of Maia") refers to Mercury, whom Jupiter *demittit* (3rd sg. pres., "sends down") *ab alto* (abl. of separation, "from on high/heaven"). Jupiter commands Mercury to descend and ensure Carthage welcomes the Trojans.
298:
**ut** (conjunction) "so that"; **terrae** (noun, nominative/genitive singular or nominative plural) "lands" or "the land"; **arces** (noun, nominative plural, f.) "citadels, heights"; **pateant** (verb, present subjunctive, 3rd plural) "may lie open, be accessible"; **Karthaginis** (noun, genitive singular, f.) "of Carthage." 

Mercury is sent so that the lands and citadel heights of new Carthage may be open/welcoming to the Trojans, with purpose clauses governed by the subjunctive *pateant*.
299:
**hospitio Teucris, ne fati nescia Dido**

*hospitio* (n. abl. sg., "hospitality/welcome") – ablative of means or respect; *Teucris* (m. dat. pl., "for the Trojans") – dative of advantage; *ne* (conj., "lest") – negative purpose clause; *fati* (n. gen. sg., "of fate") – objective genitive with *nescia*; *nescia* (adj. nom. f. sg., "ignorant/unaware") – predicate adjective modifying Dido. The line expresses the purpose that Dido, unaware of fate, not keep the Trojans from hospitality.
300:
**finibus arceret: volat ille per aera magnum**

*finibus* (ablative plural of *finis*) "from the borders/territory"; *arceret* (imperfect subjunctive of *arceo*) "might keep away/exclude," expressing purpose or fear; *volat* (present indicative of *volo*) "flies"; *ille* (nominative singular) "he/that one" (referring to Mercury); *aera* (accusative singular of *aer*) "air/sky"; *magnum* (accusative singular neuter of *magnus*) "great," modifying *aera*. Mercury flies through the vast sky, lest Dido exclude the Trojans from her lands.
301:
**remigio alarum, ac Libyae citus adstitit oris.**

*remigio* (n., abl. sing.) "by the rowing/oarage" – ablative of means with *alarum* (gen. pl.) "of wings"; *Libyae* (gen. sing.) "of Libya"; *citus* (adj., nom. sing.) "swift/swiftly"; *adstitit* (perf., 3rd sing.) "he stood at/arrived at"; *oris* (n., dat./abl. pl.) "to/at the shores." Mercury flies swiftly to Libya's shores using his wings as oars.
302:
**Et iam iussa facit, ponuntque ferocia Poeni**

*iussa* (n. pl. acc., perf. pass. participle of *iubeo*): "commands, orders"; *facit* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic.): "does, carries out"; *ponunt* (3rd pl. pres. act. indic. of *pono*): "lay aside, put down"; *ferocia* (n. pl. acc., adj. used substantively): "fierce spirits, ferocity"; *Poeni* (m. pl. nom.): "the Carthaginians." Mercury's divine intervention takes immediate effect: the Carthaginians carry out Jupiter's commands and abandon their hostility toward the Trojans.
303:
**corda volente deo; in primis regina quietum**

*corda* (n. acc. pl., "hearts") – the Carthaginians' fierce hearts are softened; *volente* (pres. act. part. abl. sg., "with [god] willing") – ablative absolute with *deo* (m. abl. sg., "god"), indicating divine causation; *in primis* (adverbial phrase, "especially, first of all") – singles out Dido; *regina* (f. nom. sg., "queen") – subject; *quietum* (adj. acc. sg. m., "peaceful, calm") – predicative accusative modifying *animum* in the next line. God (Venus's influence) calms Carthaginian hostility, especially ensuring Dido receives a tranquil disposition toward the Trojans.
304:
**accipit in Teucros animum mentemque benignam.**

*accipit* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *accipiō*) "receives, takes on"; *Teucros* (acc. pl. m. of *Teucrī*) "the Trojans"; *animum* (acc. sg. m. of *animus*) "spirit, disposition"; *mentemque* (acc. sg. f. of *mēns* + *-que*) "and mind"; *benignam* (acc. sg. f. of *benignus*) "kindly, favorable." Dido receives/adopts a kindly spirit and mind toward the Trojans, her hostility giving way to benevolence with divine favor.
305:
**Target: At pius Aeneas, per noctem plurima volvens,**

*pius* (adj., nom. sg. m.) "dutiful/pious," modifying Aeneas; *per noctem* (prep. + acc. sg. f.) "through the night"; *plurima* (adj., acc. pl. n.) "very many things," object of *volvens*; *volvens* (pres. part., nom. sg. m.) "turning over/pondering," describing Aeneas's nocturnal deliberations. The line depicts Aeneas wakefully reflecting on many concerns during the night before deciding to explore the new land at dawn.
306:
**ut primum lux alma data est, exire locosque**

*ut primum* (conjunction + adverb) "as soon as"; *lux* (nom. sing., subject) "light"; *alma* (nom. sing. fem. adj.) "nurturing, life-giving"; *data est* (perf. pass. indic. 3rd sing. of *do*) "was given, has been given"; *exire* (pres. act. inf. of *exeo*) "to go out, to depart," completing the sense of purpose or intention established by *volvens* in the previous line. As soon as life-giving daylight was granted, Aeneas resolves to go forth and explore the places (*locosque*) where the wind has brought him.
307: **explorare** (infinitive, from *explōrō*) "to explore, reconnoiter"; **novos** (acc. masc. pl. of *novus*) "new" modifying *locosque*; **quas** (acc. fem. pl. relative pronoun) "which" referring to *oras*; **vento** (abl. masc. sg. of *ventus*) "by/with the wind"; **accesserit** (perf. subj. 3rd sg. of *accēdō*) "he/she has approached"; **oras** (acc. fem. pl. of *ōra*) "shores, coasts." Aeneas resolves to explore new lands and discover which shores he has reached by the wind's force.
308:
**qui teneant, nam inculta videt, hominesne feraene,**

*qui* (relative pronoun, nom. pl. m.) "who"; *teneant* (pres. subj. act. 3rd pl. of *teneo*) "hold/inhabit" (subjunctive in indirect question); *inculta* (acc. pl. n. of *incultus, -a, -um*) "uncultivated (lands)"; *videt* (pres. ind. act. 3rd sg. of *video*) "sees/perceives"; *hominesne* (*homo, -inis* nom. pl. m. + enclitic *-ne*) "men or...?"; *feraene* (*fera, -ae* nom. pl. f. + *-ne*) "beasts?" He resolves to discover who inhabit these shores, since he sees uncultivated lands
309: **quaerere** (present active infinitive, "to seek/investigate") **constituit** (3rd sing. perfect indicative of *constituo*, "he resolved/decided"), **sociis** (dative plural of *socius*, "to his companions"), **exacta** (perfect passive participle, neuter plural accusative, "things ascertained/learned"), **referre** (present active infinitive, "to report/bring back"). Aeneas resolves to investigate the land and report back to his companions what he has learned exactly.
310: **Classem** (acc. sg., "fleet") **in convexo** (abl. sg., "in the hollow/curved recess") **nemorum** (gen. pl., "of the groves") **sub rupe cavata** (abl. sg., "beneath a hollowed-out cliff"). Aeneas discovers his ships sheltered in a natural harbor formed by a curved grove beneath an overhanging, cave-like rock formation.
311: **arboribus** (abl. pl., f., *arbor*) "with/by trees" – ablative of means; **clausam** (acc. sg. f., perf. pass. part. of *claudo*) "enclosed, shut in" – modifying *classem* from the previous line; **circum** (adv./prep.) "around, on all sides"; **horrentibus** (abl. pl., pres. act. part. of *horreo*) "bristling, shaggy, gloomy"; **umbris** (abl. pl., f., *umbra*) "with shadows." The fleet is hidden, enclosed all around by trees and dark, threatening shadows.
312:
**occulit; ipse uno graditur comitatus Achate,**

*occulit* (3rd sg. pres. act. indic. of *occulo*, "conceals/hides") – Aeneas hides the ships in the enclosed harbor. *ipse* (nom. sg. masc. intensive pron., "he himself") emphasizes Aeneas acting alone. *graditur* (3rd sg. pres. dep. indic. of *gradior*, "walks/proceeds") describes his movement. *comitatus* (nom. sg. masc. perf. pass. part. of *comitor*, "accompanied") modifies *ipse*. *Achate* (abl. sg. of *Achates*, "Achates") – accompanied by one companion, his faithful Achates.
313: **bina** (distributive numeral, neuter accusative plural) "two each/a pair of"; **manu** (noun, ablative singular) "in/with his hand"; **crispans** (present participle, nominative singular) "brandishing, waving"; **hastilia** (noun, neuter accusative plural) "spear-shafts, javelins"; **ferro** (noun, ablative singular) "with iron/blade," modifying *lato* "broad." Aeneas brandishes a pair of broad-bladed spears, one in each hand, as he walks accompanied only by Achates.
314: **Cui** (dat. sg., relative/interrogative pronoun) "to whom"; **mater** (nom. sg.) "mother"; **sese** (acc. sg., reflexive pronoun) "herself"; **tulit** (3rd sg. perf. act., *fero*) "bore, carried"; **obvia** (nom. sg. fem. adj.) "meeting, in the way of." The mother (Diana) bore herself to meet [Camilla] in the midst of the forest, presenting herself as an encounter.
315: **virginis** (gen. sg. fem., "of a maiden") modifies both *os* and *habitum*, while **os** (acc. sg. neut., "face") and **habitumque** (acc. sg. masc., "and garb/appearance") serve as objects of the participle *gerens* ("wearing, bearing"). **gerens** (pres. part. nom. sg., "wearing") and **arma** (acc. pl. neut., "arms, weapons") complete the description of Venus disguised as a Spartan huntress, bearing both the face and dress of a maiden along with a maiden's hunting equipment.
316:
**Spartanae**: adjective, genitive singular feminine, modifying an implied "virginis" from the previous line; "of a Spartan (maiden)," referring to a Spartan girl or woman.

**equos**: noun, accusative plural masculine (from "equus"); "horses," direct object of "fatigat."

**Threissa**: adjective, nominative singular feminine; "Thracian (woman)," referring to a woman from Thrace.

**fatigat**: verb, 3rd person singular present active indicative (from "fatigo"); "wearies" or "exercises," describing the action of training horses.

This line presents two comparisons for Camilla: either like a Spartan maiden, or like a Thracian woman who trains horses.
317: **Harpalyce** (nom. sing., proper noun) – Harpalyce, a Thracian princess famed for her swiftness; **volucrem** (acc. sing. adj.) – "swift-flowing" or "winged," modifying Hebrum; **fuga** (abl. sing.) – "in flight/speed"; **praevertitur** (3rd sing. pres. pass. indic.) – "she outstrips/surpasses"; **Hebrum** (acc. sing., proper noun) – the Hebrus river. The line compares Camilla to Harpalyce, who in her speed surpasses even the swift-flowing Hebrus river of Thrace.
318:
**Namque umeris de more habilem suspenderat arcum**

*namque* (conjunction) "for indeed"; *umeris* (masculine plural ablative, *umerus*) "from/on the shoulders"; *de more* (prepositional phrase with ablative, *mos*) "according to custom, in her usual manner"; *habilem* (masculine/feminine singular accusative, *habilis*) "fitted, ready for use"; *suspenderat* (pluperfect active indicative, *suspendere*) "she had hung"; *arcum* (masculine singular accusative, *arcus*) "bow." The warrior-huntress had hung her ready bow from her shoulders in her customary fashion.
319:
**venatrix, dederatque comam diffundere ventis,**

*venatrix* (nom. sing. fem., "huntress") – describes Dido's appearance as a hunter. *dederat* (pluperfect, 3rd sing., from *do*, "she had given/allowed") governs the infinitive *diffundere* ("to scatter/stream"). *comam* (acc. sing. fem., "hair") is the object of *diffundere*. *ventis* (dat. pl. masc., "to the winds") is dative complement with *diffundere*. Dido had allowed her hair to flow freely in the winds, completing the image of her as an active, unencumbered huntress.
320:
**nuda genu, nodoque sinus collecta fluentis.**

*nuda* (adj., nom. fem. sing.) "bare"; *genu* (noun, abl. neut. sing.) "as to the knee"; *nodo* (noun, abl. masc. sing.) "with/by a knot"; *sinus* (noun, acc. masc. pl.) "folds (of her garment)"; *collecta* (perf. pass. participle, nom. fem. sing.) "gathered/bound up"; *fluentis* (pres. participle, acc. masc. pl.) "flowing." This describes the huntress Diana-like maiden (actually Venus in disguise) with her knee bare and the flowing folds of her dress gathered up in a knot for ease of movement.
321:
**Gloss:**

*Heus* (interjection): "Hey!" or "Ho there!", an exclamatory address to get attention. *iuvenes* (nom. pl. m., "iuvenis"): "young men," the addressees. *monstrate* (2nd pl. imperative, "monstro"): "show" or "point out," commanding them to indicate. *mearum* (gen. pl. f., "meus"): "of my [sisters]," possessive modifying the implied *sororum*. *prior* (nom. sg. f., "prior"): "first" or "taking the initiative," describing the speaker (likely Venus disguised as a huntress) who speaks before the young men can reply. *inquit* (3rd sg., "inquio"): "she says" or "she said," the standard verb for introducing direct speech.
322: **vidistis** (perfect active indicative, 2nd person plural of *video*) "have you seen"; **quam** (accusative singular feminine of *quis*, interrogative adjective modifying *sororem*) "which/any"; **errantem** (present active participle, accusative singular feminine of *erro*) "wandering"; **forte** (adverb) "by chance/perhaps"; **sororum** (genitive plural of *soror*) "of [my] sisters." Dido asks the young men if they have perhaps seen any of her sisters wandering here.
323: **succinctam** (perfect passive participle, accusative singular feminine of *succingō*) "girded up, tucked up"; **pharetrā** (ablative singular of *pharetra*, -ae) "with a quiver"; **maculōsae** (genitive singular feminine of *maculōsus*, -a, -um) "spotted"; **tegmine** (ablative singular of *tegmen*, -inis, neuter) "with the hide/skin"; **lyncis** (genitive singular of *lynx*, lyncis) "of a lynx." Venus (disguised as a huntress) describes the typical appearance of one of Diana's companions: dressed in hunting attire with a quiver and wearing a spotted lynx-skin.
324: **aut** (conj.) "or"; **spumantis** (pres. part. gen. sg. m., from *spumo*) "foaming/frothing," modifying *apri*; **apri** (gen. sg. m., *aper*) "of a boar"; **cursum** (acc. sg. m., *cursus*) "the chase/course"; **clamore** (abl. sg. m., *clamor*) "with shouting"; **prementem** (pres. part. acc. sg. f., *premo*) "pressing/pursuing," agreeing with the subject (likely Dido). The line depicts her either pursuing the foaming boar's flight with shouting, an image of vigorous hunting.
325:
**Gloss:**

*Venus* (nom. sg.): the goddess Venus, subject of elliptical verb "spoke" implied by *sic*. *contra* (adv.): "in reply, in response." *filius* (nom. sg.): "son," referring to Aeneas. *orsus* (perf. part. of *ordior*, nom. sg. masc.): "having begun (to speak), commenced," a deponent verb governing indirect discourse. Venus speaks thus, and in reply her son thus began speaking.
326: **Nulla** (nom. sing. fem., "none") agrees with the understood subject; **tuarum...sororum** (gen. pl. fem., "of your sisters") modifies it; **audita** (nom. sing. fem., perfect passive participle of *audio*, "heard") and **visa** (nom. sing. fem., perfect passive participle of *video*, "seen") serve as predicates; **mihi** (dat. sing., "by me") indicates the agent with the passive participles. Aeneas declares that none of the maiden's sisters has been heard or seen by him, preparing to ask her identity.
327: **memorem** (1st sg. pres. subj. act. of *memoro*, "call/name"), **virgo** (voc. sg., "maiden"), **haud** (adv., "not at all"), **voltus** (nom. sg., "face/countenance"). Aeneas asks how he should address this mysterious maiden, noting that her appearance is not mortal.
328: **mortalis** (adj., nom. sg. fem.) "mortal"; **vox** (n., nom. sg. fem.) "voice"; **hominem** (n., acc. sg. masc.) "human being"; **sonat** (v., 3rd sg. pres. ind. act.) "sounds (like)"; **dea** (n., nom. sg. fem.) "goddess"; **certe** (adv.) "certainly." Aeneas declares that the maiden's appearance is not mortal, nor does her voice sound like a human's—she is certainly a goddess.
329: **an** (conjunction): "or" (introducing alternative questions). **Phoebi** (genitive singular, proper noun): "of Phoebus/Apollo." **soror** (nominative singular, noun): "sister" (i.e., Diana). **nympharum** (genitive plural, noun): "of the nymphs." **sanguinis** (genitive singular, noun): "of the blood/lineage." Aeneas poses two alternatives: is she Apollo's sister (Diana), or one sprung from nymphs' blood?
330: **sis** (2nd sg. pres. subj. of *sum*) "may you be"; **felix** (nom. sg. adj.) "happy, fortunate"; **leves** (2nd sg. pres. subj. of *levo, levare*) "may you lighten, relieve"; **laborem** (acc. sg. m. of *labor*) "toil, hardship"; **quaecumque** (nom. sg. f. of *quicumque*) "whoever you are." Aeneas wishes the maiden happiness and asks that she, whoever she may be, lighten their present struggle.
331: **et** (conj.) "and"; **quo** (abl. interrog. adj. modifying "caelo") "under what"; **caelo** (abl. n. sg. of "caelum") "sky, heaven"; **tandem** (adv.) "finally, pray"; **quibus** (abl. interrog. adj. modifying "oris") "in what"; **orbis** (gen. sg. of "orbis") "of the world, circle"; **oris** (abl. f. pl. of "ora") "shores, regions." Aeneas asks under what sky and in what regions of the world they are being tossed about, continuing his plea to the Sibyl for guidance in their wanderings.
332:
**iactemur, doceas. Ignari hominumque locorumque**

*iactemur* (1st pl. pres. subjunctive passive of *iacio*): "we are tossed about" (purpose or result clause); *doceas* (2nd sg. pres. subjunctive of *doceo*): "may you teach/tell" (jussive or purpose); *ignari* (nom. pl. masc. adj.): "ignorant (of), not knowing"; *hominumque* (*hominum* + *-que*): gen. pl. of *homo*, "of men/people, and"; *locorumque* (*locorum* + *-que*): gen. pl. of *locus*, "of places, and." The speaker asks to be informed while admitting ignorance of both the inhabitants and geography, with the genitives governed by *ignari*.
333: **erramus** (1st pl. pres. ind. act. of *erro*, "we wander/stray"), **vento** (abl. sg. masc. of *ventus*, "by wind"), **vastis** (abl. pl. masc./neut. of *vastus*, "vast/immense," modifying *fluctibus*), **fluctibus** (abl. pl. masc. of *fluctus*, "by waves"), **acti** (nom. pl. masc. perf. pass. part. of *ago*, "driven"). The Trojans explain their wandering driven by wind and vast waves to this place.
334: **hostia** (nom. sg. f., "victim, sacrificial animal") is the subject; **cadet** (3rd sg. fut. act., *cadō*, "will fall") is the main verb; **ante aras** (acc. pl. f. with prep., "before the altars") locates the sacrifice; **dextra** (abl. sg. f., "by [my] right hand") indicates agency; **tibi** (dat. sg., "for you") marks the beneficiary. Dido promises that many victims will be sacrificed at the altars in honor of her divine guest.
335: **Haud** (adv.) "not at all, by no means"; **equidem** (adv.) "indeed, for my part"; **tali** (abl. sg. m./n. of *talis*) "such" modifying *honore*; **dignor** (1st sg. pres. pass. indic. of *dignor*, deponent) "I deem myself worthy"; **honore** (abl. sg. m. of *honor*) "honor, distinction." Dido protests she does not consider herself worthy of such honor (being compared to Diana), then Venus responds with "Tum Venus" introducing her reply.
336:
**virginibus** (dat. pl. f., *virgo*) "for maidens"; **Tyriis** (dat. pl. f., *Tyrius*) "Tyrian"; **mos** (nom. sg. m., *mos*) "custom, practice"; **gestare** (pres. inf., *gesto*) "to carry, wear"; **pharetram** (acc. sg. f., *pharetra*) "quiver." 

Venus explains that it is the custom for Tyrian maidens to carry a quiver, justifying the armed appearance of the disguised goddess (or her companion nymphs).
337:
**purpureoque alte suras vincire cothurno.**

*purpureo* (adjective, ablative singular masculine/neuter, modifying *cothurno*) "purple, crimson"; *alte* (adverb) "high up"; *suras* (noun, accusative plural feminine) "calves (of the leg)"; *vincire* (infinitive) "to bind, tie"; *cothurno* (noun, ablative singular masculine) "hunting boot, buskin." It is the Tyrian custom for maidens to bind their calves high up with the purple hunting boot.
338:
**Punica regna vides, Tyrios et Agenoris urbem;**

*Punica* (adj. neut. pl. acc.) "Carthaginian"; *regna* (n. neut. pl. acc.) "kingdoms, realm"; *vides* (2nd sg. pres. indic.) "you see"; *Tyrios* (adj. masc. pl. acc.) "Tyrian"; *Agenoris* (m. gen. sg.) "of Agenor" (father of Dido's ancestor Cadmus); *urbem* (f. acc. sg.) "city." Venus shows Aeneas the Carthaginian territories and the Tyrian city founded by descendants of Agenor.
339:
**sed fines Libyci, genus intractabile bello.**

*fines* (m. acc. pl., "borders/territory"), *Libyci* (adj. nom. pl., "Libyan"), *genus* (n. nom. sg., "race/people"), *intractabile* (adj. nom. sg., "intractable/unmanageable"), *bello* (n. abl. sg., "in war"). The borders are Libyan, but the native people are fierce and ungovernable in warfare—Virgil contrasts Dido's Tyrian foundation with the hostile indigenous population surrounding Carthage.
340:
**Imperium Dido Tyria regit urbe profecta,**

*Imperium* (n., acc. sg.): "kingdom/power"; *Dido* (proper n., nom. sg.): the Phoenician queen; *Tyria* (adj., abl. sg. f.): "from Tyre/Tyrian," modifying *urbe*; *regit* (v., 3rd sg. pres.): "rules/governs"; *urbe* (n., abl. sg.): "from the city"; *profecta* (perf. part., nom. sg. f.): "having set out/departed." Dido, having departed from the Tyrian city, rules the kingdom (Carthage).
341:
**germanum fugiens. Longa est iniuria, longae**

*germanum* (m. acc. sg., "brother," object of *fugiens*); *fugiens* (pres. part., "fleeing"); *longa* (f. nom. sg., "long, lengthy," modifying *iniuria*); *iniuria* (f. nom. sg., "wrong, injustice," subject of *est*); *longae* (f. nom./gen. sg., likely gen. with ellipsis, "of long [story/tale]"). Dido flees her brother; the injustice done is long (to recount), as are the deceptions/wanderings (understood with *longae*).
342: **ambages** (nom. pl. f.) "windings, digressions" – **sed** (conj.) "but" – **summa** (acc. pl. n.) "highest points, main events" – **sequar** (fut. 1st sg. dep.) "I shall follow" – **fastigia** (acc. pl. n.) "peaks, chief points" – **rerum** (gen. pl. f.) "of events, matters." The narrator acknowledges the long story (*longae ambages*) but promises to follow only the main points; *summa fastigia* forms a hendiadys for "highest peaks" or "essential narrative."
343:
**Huic coniunx Sychaeus erat, ditissimus agri**

*Huic* (demonstrative dative, "to this [woman]," i.e., Dido) takes *coniunx* (nominative, "husband") as subject with *Sychaeus* (nominative proper name) in apposition; *erat* (imperfect "was"); *ditissimus* (superlative nominative masculine, "richest") governs the genitive *agri* ("of land/territory"). Sychaeus was Dido's husband, the wealthiest of the Phoenicians in landed possessions.
344:
**Phoenicum, et magno miserae dilectus amore,**

*Phoenicum* (gen. pl., "of the Phoenicians") modifies *agri* from the previous line, indicating Sychaeus was wealthiest in Phoenician lands. *miserae* (dat. sg. fem., "by/for the wretched [woman]," i.e., Dido). *dilectus* (perf. pass. partic. nom. sg. m., "loved/beloved") agrees with Sychaeus. *magno...amore* (abl. sg., "with great love") describes the manner of his being beloved by the ill-fated Dido.
345: **cui** (relative/indirect object, dative) "to whom"; **pater** (nominative subject) "father"; **intactam** (accusative feminine, modifying an understood object like *filiam*) "untouched, virgin"; **dederat** (pluperfect active) "had given"; **iugarat** (pluperfect active) "had joined in marriage." Dido's father had given her as a virgin bride to Sychaeus and joined them in first marriage (the dative *cui* refers back to Sychaeus from the previous line, and *primis* modifies the understood nuptial rites).
346:
**ominibus. Sed regna Tyri germanus habebat**

*ominibus* (n. pl. abl.) – "omens, auspices"; ablative of attendant circumstance with *primis* from the previous line, indicating the marriage was performed with proper auspices. *Sed* – adversative conjunction, "but," marking a turn to the conflict. *regna* (n. pl. acc.) – "kingdom, power," direct object of *habebat*. *Tyri* (gen. sg.) – "of Tyre," genitive of place. *germanus* (m. nom. sg.) – "brother," subject; here Pygmalion, Dido's brother, held royal power in Tyre.
347:
**Pygmalion, scelere ante alios immanior omnes.**

*Pygmalion* (nom. sg. m., proper name) = Pygmalion, Dido's brother; *scelere* (abl. sg. n., from *scelus*) = in crime/wickedness (respect); *ante* (prep. + acc.) = before, beyond; *alios* (acc. pl. m., from *alius*) = others; *immanior* (nom. sg. m., comparative adj. from *immanis*) = more monstrous/savage; *omnes* (acc. pl. m., from *omnis*) = all. Pygmalion is described as more monstrous in crime than all others, establishing his villainy before narrating his murder of Sychaeus.
348:
**Quos inter medius venit furor. Ille Sychaeum**

*Quos* (relative pronoun, acc. pl. masc., "whom"); *inter* (preposition + acc., "between, among"); *medius* (adjective, nom. sg. masc., "in the middle of"); *furor* (noun, nom. sg., "madness, rage"); *venit* (verb, perf. 3rd sg., "came"). Between these men came madness in their midst—namely, Pygmalion's murderous rage aimed at Sychaeus, Dido's husband.
349:
**impius ante aras, atque auri caecus amore,**

*impius* (nom. sg. m., adj.): "impious, wicked" (modifying the subject, Pygmalion); *ante aras* (acc. pl. f. with prep.): "before the altars," emphasizing sacrilege; *auri* (gen. sg. n.): "of gold," objective genitive with *amore*; *caecus* (nom. sg. m., adj.): "blind," metaphorically describing moral blindness; *amore* (abl. sg. m.): "by/with love," ablative of cause. Pygmalion's crime is doubly condemned: he murders at the sacred altars, blinded by gold-lust.
350:
**clam** (adv.) "secretly"; **ferro** (abl. sg. n.) "with a sword/weapon"; **incautum** (acc. sg. m.) "unsuspecting, off his guard"; **superat** (3rd sg. pres.) "he overcomes, kills"; **securus** (nom. sg. m.) "heedless, unconcerned" (+ gen. **amorum** "of the love/affection"). 

Pygmalion secretly kills the unsuspecting Sychaeus with a sword, unconcerned about his sister's love for her husband.
351: **germanae** (gen. sg. or dat. sg. of *germana*, "sister"): genitive singular depending on context, "of [his] sister" (Dido). **factum** (acc. sg. n. of *factum*, "deed"): "the deed," direct object of *celavit*. **celavit** (3rd sg. perf. act. ind. of *celo*, "to hide/conceal"): "he concealed." **aegram** (acc. sg. f. of *aeger*, "sick/lovesick"): modifying an understood Dido, "the sick/suffering [woman]," coordinated with *germanae* as objects of the deception. Sychaeus' murderer (Pygmalion) long concealed the crime from his sister and deceived the lovesick Dido with false hopes.
352:
**multa** (acc. pl. neut., "many things") **malus** (nom. sg. masc., "evil/wicked") **simulans** (pres. part., "feigning/pretending") **lusit** (perf. 3rd sg., "mocked/deceived") **amantem** (acc. sg. masc./fem., "the lover"). 

The wicked man, feigning many things, deceived the lover with false hope; Sychaeus concealed his murder from Dido and cruelly misled her with empty expectations.
353: **Ipsa** (nom. sg. fem. intensive pronoun) "she herself"; **somnis** (abl. pl. m., *somnus*) "in dreams/sleep"; **inhumati** (gen. sg. m., perfect passive participle of *inhumo*) "of the unburied one"; **imago** (nom. sg. fem.) "ghost/phantom/shade"; **venit** (3rd sg. pres./perf. indic., *venio*) "comes/came." The ghost of the unburied husband himself appeared to her in dreams, with *ipsa* emphasizing the direct visitation and *inhumati* stressing his unmourned, unburied state that motivates his supernatural appearance.
354: **coniugis** (genitive singular of *coniunx*) "of her husband" – depends on *imago* from the previous line. **ora** (accusative plural neuter of *os*) "face" or "features" – direct object of *attollens*. **attollens** (present active participle, nominative singular) "lifting up" or "raising" – modifies *imago*. **pallida** (accusative plural neuter of *pallidus*) "pale" – adjective modifying *ora*. **modis...miris** (ablative plural of *modus* and *mirus*) "in wondrous/strange ways" – ablative of manner. The ghost of her husband raises up pale features in an extraordinary manner.
355:
**crudeles aras traiectaque pectora ferro**

*crudeles* (adj., acc. pl. f.) "cruel" modifies *aras*; *aras* (noun, acc. pl. f.) "altars"; *traiecta* (perf. pass. part., acc. pl. n.) "pierced through" modifies *pectora*; *pectora* (noun, acc. pl. n.) "breasts/chests"; *ferro* (noun, abl. sg. n.) "by/with iron/sword," ablative of means. Aeneas sees the cruel altars and the breasts pierced through by the sword, revealing the household crime.
356: **nudavit** (perfect, 3rd sing. from *nudo*) "laid bare, revealed"; **caecum** (acc. neut. sing., adj.) "hidden, blind"; **domus** (gen. sing.) "of the house"; **scelus** (acc. neut. sing.) "crime"; **retexit** (perfect, 3rd sing. from *retego*) "uncovered, disclosed." The subject (likely Creusa's ghost or a divine informant) exposed all the hidden crime of the household, laying bare what had been concealed.
357: **Tum** (adv.) "then"; **celerare** (inf., complementary) "to hasten"; **fugam** (acc. sg. f.) "flight, escape"; **patriaque** (abl. sg. f., = *et patria*) "and from the fatherland"; **excedere** (inf., complementary) "to depart." Anchises urges swift departure from Troy, with both infinitives depending on *suadet* (he advises/urges).
358:
**auxiliumque viae veteres tellure recludit**

*auxiliumque* (n. acc. sg., "and aid/help") connects with *viae* (gen. sg., "for the journey"); *veteres* (adj. acc. pl., "ancient [treasures]"); *tellure* (abl. sg., "from/in the earth"); *recludit* (3rd sg. pres., "he opens up/reveals"). Anchises reveals ancient treasures hidden in the earth as assistance for their journey, providing them with the wealth described in the next line.
359:
**thesauros, ignotum argenti pondus et auri.**

*thesauros* (acc. pl. m., "treasures"), *ignotum* (acc. sg. n., "unknown/hidden," modifying *pondus*), *argenti* (gen. sg. n., "of silver"), *pondus* (acc. sg. n., "weight/mass"), *auri* (gen. sg. n., "of gold"). Dido uncovers treasures—a hidden weight/hoard of silver and gold—from the earth to finance her flight.
360:
**His commota fugam Dido sociosque parabat:**

*His* (ablative plural, demonstrative pronoun) "by these things"; *commota* (perfect passive participle, nominative singular feminine from commoveo) "moved/stirred"; *fugam* (accusative singular feminine) "flight/escape"; *Dido* (nominative singular) "Dido" (subject); *parabat* (3rd singular imperfect active from paro) "was preparing." Moved by these circumstances, Dido was preparing flight and gathering allies/companions (socios, accusative plural masculine) for their escape from the tyrant.
361:
**conveniunt, quibus aut odium crudele tyranni**

*conveniunt* (3rd pl. pres. ind. act. of *convenio*) "they assemble/gather"; *quibus* (dat. pl. of relative pronoun *qui*) "for whom"; *odium* (nom. sg. neut. noun) "hatred"; *crudele* (nom. sg. neut. adj.) "cruel"; *tyranni* (gen. sg. masc. noun) "of the tyrant." Those assemble for whom either cruel hatred of the tyrant (Pygmalion) or keen fear was the motive for fleeing with Dido.
362: **aut** (conj.) "or"; **metus** (nom. sg. m.) "fear"; **acer** (nom. sg. m. adj.) "sharp, keen"; **paratae** (nom. pl. f. perf. pass. part. from *paro*) "prepared, ready." The line continues the description of those who joined Aeneas—either driven by cruel hatred of the tyrant or by sharp fear—and mentions ships which happened to be ready at hand.
363:
**corripiunt, onerantque auro: portantur avari**

*corripiunt* (3rd pl. pres. ind. act., *corripio*) "they seize"; *onerantque* (3rd pl. pres. ind. act., *onero* + *-que*) "and they load"; *auro* (abl. sg. n., *aurum*) "with gold"; *portantur* (3rd pl. pres. ind. pass., *porto*) "are carried"; *avari* (nom. pl. m., *avarus*) "the greedy one's [wealth]" or "the miser's [treasures]." The Carthaginian refugees seize the prepared ships, load them with Pygmalion's gold, and carry off the wealth of the greedy tyrant across the sea.
364:
**Pygmalionis opes pelago; dux femina facti.**

*Pygmalionis* (gen. sing., "of Pygmalion") – the possessive genitive naming Dido's brother, whose wealth is being carried off. *opes* (acc. pl., "riches, resources") – direct object of the implied verb of carrying from the previous line. *pelago* (dat./abl. sing., "by/on the sea") – ablative of means indicating how the wealth is transported. *dux* (nom. sing., "leader") – predicate noun describing the woman. *femina* (nom. sing., "woman") – in apposition to *dux*, emphasizing Dido's role. *facti* (gen. sing., "of the deed") – objective genitive with *dux*, marking her as leader of this escape/enterprise.
365:
**Devenere locos, ubi nunc ingentia cernis**

*Devenere* (perfect, 3rd pl. "they came/arrived"), *locos* (acc. pl. "places/site"), *ubi* (relative adv. "where"), *ingentia* (acc. pl. neut. "huge [walls/structures]"), *cernis* (2nd sg. pres. "you see"). The Trojan refugees arrived at the place where now (the reader's present) one sees the massive walls of Carthage; Virgil directly addresses the reader to mark the contrast between humble beginnings and Rome's future rival.
366:
**moenia surgentemque novae Karthaginis arcem**

*moenia* (n. acc. pl.): "walls, fortifications"; *surgentem* (pres. part. acc. sg. f.): "rising"; *novae* (adj. gen. sg. f.): "new," modifying *Karthaginis*; *Karthaginis* (gen. sg.): "of Carthage"; *arcem* (acc. sg. f.): "citadel, fortress." Aeneas arrives at the place where he now sees the massive walls and the rising citadel of new Carthage.
367:
**mercatique solum, facti de nomine Byrsam,**

*mercati* (perf. part. of *mercor*, nom. pl. masc.) "having purchased"; *solum* (acc. sg. neut.) "land, ground"; *facti* (perf. part. of *facio*, gen. sg. neut., agreeing with *nomine*) "made, done"; *nomine* (abl. sg. neut.) "from the name"; *Byrsam* (acc. sg. fem.) "Byrsa," the citadel of Carthage, from Greek *byrsa* meaning "hide." The Phoenicians purchased land and named it Byrsa after the oxhide (*taurino tergo*) they cut into strips to encircle the maximum territory.
368:
**taurino quantum possent circumdare tergo.**

*taurino* (adj., ablative singular neuter, modifying *tergo*) "of a bull"; *quantum* (adv.) "as much as"; *possent* (verb, imperfect subjunctive, 3rd plural) "they could"; *circumdare* (verb, present infinitive) "to encircle, encompass"; *tergo* (noun, ablative singular neuter) "hide, skin." The line explains the etymological legend of Byrsa: the Tyrians purchased as much land as they could encircle with a bull's hide (cut into thin strips).
369:
**Gloss on "Sed vos qui tandem, quibus aut venistis ab oris":**

*vos* (2nd pers. pl. pronoun, nom.) "you"; *tandem* (adv.) "finally, pray tell"; *quibus* (interrog. adj., abl. pl.) "from what"; *venistis* (2nd pl. perf. act. indic. of *venio*) "have you come"; *oris* (abl. pl. of *ora*, -ae, f.) "shores, lands." Dido interrogates her Trojan visitors, asking who they are and from what lands they have come.
370:
**quove tenetis iter? Quaerenti talibus ille**

*quo-ve* (adverb): "or to where," ablative of direction. *tenetis* (2nd pl. pres. act. indic. of *teneo*): "you hold/steer," governing *iter*. *iter* (nom./acc. neut. sg.): "journey, course." *quaerenti* (pres. act. participle dat. sg. of *quaero*): "to (him) asking," referring to Aeneas. *talibus* (abl. neut. pl. of *talis*): "with such (words)," modifying the unspoken *verbis*. *ille* (nom. sg. masc.): "that one/he," the subject of *suspirans* in the next line.

Aeneas asks "where are you heading?" and one of the strangers
371:
**suspirans, imoque trahens a pectore vocem:**

*suspirans* (pres. part., nom. sg. m.) "sighing"; *imo* (adj., abl. sg. n.) "deepest, lowest"; *trahens* (pres. part., nom. sg. m.) "drawing"; *pectore* (noun, abl. sg. n.) "from the chest/heart"; *vocem* (noun, acc. sg. f.) "voice, words." Aeneas responds with a sigh, drawing his voice from the depths of his heart, expressing the emotional weight of recounting Troy's fall.
372:
**Gloss for *O dea, si prima repetens ab origine pergam*:**

*dea* (voc. sg. fem., "goddess") addresses Dido; *prima...ab origine* (abl. sg. fem., "from the first beginning") marks the chronological starting point; *repetens* (pres. part. nom. sg. masc., "recounting, going back over") modifies the subject Aeneas; *pergam* (pres. subj. 1st sg., "I should proceed") forms the apodosis of the conditional introduced by *si*. Aeneas hesitates before narrating Troy's fall, suggesting the tale would be too long if told from the very beginning.
373:
**Gloss for *et vacet annalis nostrorum audire laborum*:**

*vacet* (pres. subj. 3rd sg. of *vacare*) "there be time/leisure"; *annalis* (acc. pl. m. of *annalis, -e*) "yearly [accounts]" or "the annals"; *audire* (pres. inf. of *audire*) "to hear"; *laborum* (gen. pl. of *labor, -oris*) "of our toils/sufferings." Aeneas suggests that even if there were time to hear the complete yearly record of the Trojans' hardships, evening (Vesper) would close Olympus before he could finish.
374:
**ante diem clauso componat Vesper Olympo.**

Key words: *ante* (preposition + accusative) "before"; *diem* (accusative singular of *dies*) "day"; *clauso* (ablative singular perfect passive participle of *claudo*) "closed, shut"; *componat* (3rd singular present subjunctive of *compono*) "may settle, lay to rest"; *Vesper* (nominative singular) "the Evening Star, Hesperus"; *Olympo* (ablative singular of *Olympus*) "Olympus, heaven." Aeneas wishes that Hesperus may lay him to rest before day ends, with Olympus closed—a prayer for death before having to recount Troy's fall.
375:
**Nos Troia antiqua, si vestras forte per auris**

*Nos* (1st pl. nom. pronoun, "we"), *Troia* (abl. sg., "from Troy"), *antiqua* (abl. sg. fem. adj., "ancient"), *vestras* (acc. pl. fem. adj., "your"), *forte* (adv., "by chance/perhaps"), *auris* (acc. pl. fem., "ears"). The Trojans identify themselves as survivors from ancient Troy, asking if report of their name has perhaps reached the listeners' ears—introducing their fame and suffering before mentioning their scattered wanderings.
376: **Troiae** (gen. sg., "of Troy") **nomen** (nom. sg., "name/fame") **iit** (perf. 3rd sg. of *eo*, "went/came"), **diversa** (acc. pl. neut., "diverse/far-flung") **per aequora** (acc. pl. neut., "through seas") **vectos** (acc. pl. masc. perf. pass. part. of *veho*, "carried/conveyed"). The fame of Troy reached your ears, (us) having been carried across distant seas.
377:
**forte** (adv.) "by chance"; **sua** (poss. adj., abl. fem. sing.) "his own"; **Libycis...oris** (adj. + noun, abl. fem. pl.) "to/on Libyan shores"; **tempestas** (noun, nom. fem. sing.) "storm"; **adpulit** (verb, perf. 3rd sing.) "drove/cast."

Aeneas explains that a storm by chance drove him to the Libyan shores, providing the immediate cause of his arrival in Dido's realm.
378:
**Sum** (1st sg. pres. ind. of *sum*) "I am"; **pius** (nom. sg. m. adj.) "dutiful, pious"; **Aeneas** (nom. sg. m.) "Aeneas"; **raptos** (acc. pl. m. perf. pass. part. of *rapio*) "snatched, rescued"; **Penates** (acc. pl. m.) "household gods"; **ex hoste** (abl. sg. m. with prep.) "from the enemy."

Aeneas identifies himself with his defining epithet *pius* and claims his rescue of Troy's sacred Penates from the Greeks, establishing his divine mission and justifying his flight.
379: **classe** (abl. sing. f., *classis*) "with my fleet"; **veho** (1st sing. pres. act. indic., *vehere*) "I carry"; **mecum** (prep. + abl. pron.) "with me"; **fama** (abl. sing. f., *fama*) "by/in fame"; **aethera** (acc. sing. n., *aether*) "the heavens/sky"; **notus** (nom. sing. m., perf. pass. part., *noscere*) "known." Aeneas declares he carries (the Penates) with his fleet, himself renowned in fame beyond the heavens.
380: **Italiam** (acc. sg. f., goal of motion) "Italy," **quaero** (1st sg. pres. act. indic.) "I seek," **patriam** (acc. sg. f., apposition to Italiam) "fatherland," **genus** (acc. sg. n., direct object) "lineage/descent," **summo** (abl. sg. m., modifying Iove) "highest/supreme." Aeneas declares he seeks Italy as his destined homeland and traces his ancestry from Jupiter himself, establishing both his divine pedigree and his mission's legitimacy.
381:
**Bis denis Phrygium conscendi navibus aequor:**

*Bis denis* (adverbial phrase, "twice ten" = twenty), *Phrygium* (adjective, accusative neuter singular modifying *aequor*, "Phrygian/Trojan"), *conscendi* (perfect tense, 1st person singular of *conscendo*, "I embarked upon/boarded"), *navibus* (ablative of means, plural of *navis*, "with ships"), *aequor* (accusative neuter singular, direct object, "the sea"). Aeneas recounts how he set sail upon the Trojan sea with twenty ships.
382:
**matre dea monstrante viam, data fata secutus;**

*matre* (ablative singular, "mother") and *dea* (ablative singular, "goddess") form an ablative absolute with *monstrante* (present participle, "showing/pointing out") and *viam* (accusative, "way/course"). *data* (perfect passive participle, "given/granted") modifies *fata* (accusative neuter plural, "fates/destinies"), while *secutus* (perfect deponent participle, "having followed") completes the thought. Aeneas describes how he followed his divinely ordained destiny with his goddess-mother Venus showing him the way across the sea.
383:
**vix** (adverb) "scarcely, barely"; **septem** (numeral) "seven"; **convolsae** (perfect passive participle, nominative plural feminine, from *convello*) "torn apart, shattered"; **undis** (ablative plural of *unda*) "by the waves"; **Euroque** (ablative singular of *Eurus* with enclitic *-que*) "and by the East wind"; **supersunt** (third person plural present of *supersum*) "survive, remain." 

Aeneas laments that barely seven ships, battered by waves and the East wind, survive from his fleet.
384: **Ipse** (pronoun, nominative masculine singular): "I myself" – emphatic subject, Aeneas speaking of his own plight. **ignotus** (adjective, nominative masculine singular): "unknown, unrecognized." **egens** (present participle, nominative masculine singular): "lacking, destitute, needy." **Libyae** (noun, genitive singular): "of Libya" – modifying *deserta*. **deserta** (noun, accusative neuter plural): "deserted places, wastelands" – direct object of *peragro*. **peragro** (verb, first person singular present active indicative): "I wander through, traverse." Aeneas laments his anonymous, destitute wandering through the Libyan wilderness.
385:
**Europa atque Asia pulsus. Nec plura querentem**

*Europa* (nom. sg., f.) and *Asia* (abl. sg., f.) "from Europe and Asia"; *pulsus* (nom. sg. m., perf. pass. part. of *pello*) "driven, expelled"; *plura* (neut. acc. pl. of comparative *plus*) "more things"; *querentem* (acc. sg. m., pres. part. of *queror*) "complaining." Aeneas continues his complaint to Venus, lamenting that he has been driven from both Europe and Asia, but Venus interrupts him before he can say more.
386: **passa** (perfect participle of *patior*, nominative feminine singular) "having suffered/endured"; **Venus** (nominative singular) "Venus"; **medio...dolore** (ablative of means/manner, "in the midst of grief" or "with moderate grief"); **interfata est** (perfect deponent, *interfor*, "spoke among/interrupted"). Venus, having endured [this], thus spoke in the midst of her grief.
387:
**Quisquis es, haud, credo, invisus caelestibus auras**

*Quisquis* (indefinite pronoun, nominative singular, "whoever") *es* (2nd sg. pres. indic. of *sum*, "you are"); *haud* (adverb, "not"); *credo* (1st sg. pres. indic., "I believe"); *invisus* (perf. pass. participle/adj., nominative sg. masc., "hated, odious"); *caelestibus* (dative pl. of *caelestis*, "to the heavenly ones, gods"). Venus reassures the stranger (Aeneas in disguise) that he is not hated by the gods, since he has reached (draws in) the vital breath/airs.
388: **vitalis** (acc. pl. f., modifying *auras*) "life-giving"; **carpis** (2nd sg. pres. indic. of *carpo*) "you pluck, enjoy"; **Tyriam** (acc. sg. f., modifying *urbem*) "Tyrian, Carthaginian"; **adveneris** (2nd sg. perf. subj. of *advenio*, rel. clause of characteristic) "you who have come to"; **urbem** (acc. sg. f.) "city." Venus reassures her disguised son Aeneas that he breathes the vital air and has reached the Tyrian city, suggesting divine favor attends him.
389:
**Perge modo, atque hinc te reginae ad limina perfer**

*perge* (2nd sg. pres. imperat. of *pergo*) "proceed, go on"; *modo* (adv.) "only, just"; *hinc* (adv.) "from here"; *te* (2nd sg. acc.) "yourself"; *reginae* (gen. sg. of *regina*) "of the queen"; *limina* (acc. pl. of *limen*) "thresholds, doorway"; *perfer* (2nd sg. pres. imperat. of *perfero*) "carry, convey." Venus commands Aeneas to proceed directly from here and present himself at the queen's (Dido's) palace threshold.
390:
**Gloss for "Namque tibi reduces socios classemque relatam":**

*Namque* (conjunction): "for" or "for indeed," introducing causal explanation. *tibi* (pronoun, dative 2nd sg.): "to/for you," indicating advantage or interest. *reduces* (adjective, accusative masculine plural): "brought back" or "returned," modifying *socios*. *socios* (noun, accusative masculine plural): "companions" or "comrades," direct object. *classemque* (noun, accusative feminine singular + enclitic -*que*): "and the fleet," second direct object coordinated with *socios*. *relatam* (perfect passive participle, accusative feminine singular): "brought back," modifying *classem*.
391:
**Gloss for Aeneid line "nuntio, et in tutum versis aquilonibus actam,":**

*nuntio* (1st sg. pres. ind. act., nuntio, -are) "I announce/report"; *tutum* (neut. acc. sg., tutus, -a, -um) "safety, a safe place"; *versis* (abl. pl. perf. pass. part., verto, -ere) "with the winds having shifted/turned"; *aquilonibus* (abl. pl., aquilo, -onis, m.)
